_meta.name: BWRA starter scenario library
_meta.status: Starter scenarios drafted by RegRadar for a business-wide ML/TF risk assessment. They are prompts for the firm to adapt, not a regulator-approved list. All likelihood/impact values are DEFAULTS: configure them for your firm.
_meta.ref_note: A 'ref' only names a source where its text was checked: AMLR (Reg. (EU) 2024/1624) against docs/data/laws/32024R1624_EN.json, and the EBA ML/TF Risk Factors Guidelines (EBA/GL/2021/02 as amended by EBA/GL/2024/01) against the published amending text. Scenarios without a ref are RegRadar starter scenarios.

likelihood.d: Not expected within three years or more
Could occur about once in two to three years
Could occur about once a year
Could occur several times a year

impact.d: Absorbed in routine work, no supervisory follow-up
Supervisory finding or notable abuse, remediation plan needed
Significant breach or enabling of serious crime, sanction or business restriction likely
Systemic failure, licence at risk, major sanction or lasting reputational damage

scenarios.title: Politically exposed persons not identified or not escalated
scenarios.desc: A customer, beneficial owner or person acting for the customer is a PEP, family member or close associate and is onboarded without enhanced measures or senior sign-off.

scenarios.title: Opaque ownership structures hide the beneficial owner
scenarios.desc: Layered companies, trusts or nominee arrangements make it impossible to establish who ultimately owns or controls a business customer.

scenarios.title: Shell or newly formed companies move high volumes
scenarios.desc: Companies with no real activity, or recently incorporated entities, are used to receive and pass on large flows soon after onboarding.

scenarios.title: Money mules and straw-man account holders
scenarios.desc: Individuals who lend their identity or account to criminals, often recruited online, open accounts that are used to receive and forward proceeds.

scenarios.title: Customers in higher-risk sectors
scenarios.desc: Customers active in money services, unregulated crypto-asset services, casinos, dealing in precious metals or other cash-intensive activity are onboarded without matching enhanced measures.
scenarios.ref: EBA ML/TF Risk Factors Guidelines, Guideline 2.4(b) as replaced by EBA/GL/2024/01

scenarios.title: Non-profit organisations misused to move funds
scenarios.desc: A non-profit customer is used as a front to raise or move funds for terrorist financing or other criminal purposes.

scenarios.title: Cross-border money remittance used to move illicit funds
scenarios.desc: Fast, low-friction transfers to cash-pay-out corridors or higher-risk destinations are used to move or disguise criminal proceeds.
scenarios.ref: EBA ML/TF Risk Factors Guidelines, sectoral Guideline 11 (money remitters)

scenarios.title: Lightly verified e-money products with high load limits
scenarios.desc: Anonymous or simplified-due-diligence e-money products with generous load, spend or withdrawal limits allow value to be moved without a verified identity.
scenarios.ref: EBA ML/TF Risk Factors Guidelines, sectoral Guideline 10 (electronic money issuers)

scenarios.title: Wallets and IBANs used as pass-through accounts
scenarios.desc: Customer accounts or virtual IBANs receive funds and immediately forward them, adding an apparently legitimate layer between sender and final recipient.

scenarios.title: Merchant acquiring for high-risk or front merchants
scenarios.desc: Merchants processing through the firm are fronts, or trade in goods or services with a high abuse profile, and are onboarded without merchant-level due diligence.

scenarios.title: Payment initiation and account information services obscure fund origins
scenarios.desc: Initiated payments or aggregated account data are used to hide the true source or purpose of funds, with limited visibility of the underlying accounts.
scenarios.ref: EBA ML/TF Risk Factors Guidelines, sectoral Guideline 18 (payment initiation and account information services)

scenarios.title: Crypto-assets or services offering a higher degree of anonymity
scenarios.desc: Privacy-enhancing assets or features reduce the firm's ability to trace the origin and destination of funds.
scenarios.ref: EBA ML/TF Risk Factors Guidelines, Guideline 21.3(a), inserted by EBA/GL/2024/01

scenarios.title: Crypto-asset products with no upfront limits on volume or value
scenarios.desc: Products place no restriction on the overall volume or value of transactions a customer can make.
scenarios.ref: EBA ML/TF Risk Factors Guidelines, Guideline 21.3(c), inserted by EBA/GL/2024/01

scenarios.title: New products, features or technologies launched without a prior ML/TF assessment
scenarios.desc: A product, delivery channel, technology or customer segment goes live before its ML/TF risk has been identified, assessed and mitigated.
scenarios.ref: AMLR Art. 10(1), second subparagraph; EBA ML/TF Risk Factors Guidelines, Guideline 1.7(d), added by EBA/GL/2024/01

scenarios.title: Remote onboarding fraud: impersonation, deepfakes, synthetic identities
scenarios.desc: Fully remote onboarding is defeated with stolen, forged or AI-generated identities, so the verified person is not the real user of the account.
scenarios.ref: EBA Guidelines on remote customer onboarding solutions (EBA/GL/2022/15), referred to in Guideline 4.29 as amended by EBA/GL/2024/01

scenarios.title: Agents, distributors and introducers weaken due diligence quality
scenarios.desc: Third parties that sell or onboard on the firm's behalf apply due diligence inconsistently or are themselves complicit.

scenarios.title: Reliance on third parties or outsourced due diligence without effective oversight
scenarios.desc: Customer due diligence is performed by a provider or group entity and the firm cannot show that it is complete, current and available on request.

scenarios.title: Partner and banking-as-a-service sub-client onboarding (nested relationships)
scenarios.desc: Partners bring their own customers onto the firm's rails and the firm has limited insight into who the end users are and how they are vetted.
scenarios.ref: For CASPs: EBA ML/TF Risk Factors Guidelines, Guideline 21.3(f) (weak control over a nested service), inserted by EBA/GL/2024/01

scenarios.title: Programmatic access (APIs, bulk onboarding) enables abuse at scale
scenarios.desc: Automated onboarding or payment interfaces let a single bad actor create many accounts or move large volumes before controls can react.

scenarios.title: Customers, owners or counterparties in high-risk third countries
scenarios.desc: Customers, beneficial owners or payment counterparties are linked to countries identified as high-risk, without the required enhanced measures.

scenarios.title: Flows with jurisdictions of weak AML/CFT supervision or high corruption
scenarios.desc: Payments or customers connect to jurisdictions where supervision, transparency or the rule of law is weak, even if they are not formally listed.

scenarios.title: Cross-border activity in other Member States without local risk understanding
scenarios.desc: Customers or agents in other Member States are served on a passport basis without understanding local typologies, supervisors and national risk assessments.

scenarios.title: Evasion of targeted financial sanctions through third-country intermediaries
scenarios.desc: Sanctioned persons or sectors reach the firm indirectly via front companies, transshipment hubs or nested accounts, and screening does not catch it.
scenarios.ref: AMLR Art. 10(1): the assessment covers the risks of non-implementation and evasion of targeted financial sanctions

scenarios.title: Structuring of payments below monitoring thresholds
scenarios.desc: Amounts are split into smaller transactions, or spread across accounts and channels, to stay below reporting or alert limits.
scenarios.ref: EBA ML/TF Risk Factors Guidelines, Guideline 4.60(a) as replaced by EBA/GL/2024/01 (transactions split up to circumvent reporting limits)

scenarios.title: Rapid in-and-out movements used to layer funds
scenarios.desc: Funds enter and leave an account within hours or days with no obvious economic rationale, often through several accounts in sequence.

scenarios.title: Funding or pay-outs involving unrelated third parties
scenarios.desc: Payments come from, or go to, parties that are neither identified nor linked to the customer, with no apparent economic rationale.
scenarios.ref: For CASPs: EBA ML/TF Risk Factors Guidelines, Guideline 21.3(b), inserted by EBA/GL/2024/01

scenarios.title: Transfers to and from self-hosted wallets and unregulated providers
scenarios.desc: Customers send or receive crypto-assets to addresses that are not held by a regulated provider, which breaks the audit trail.
scenarios.ref: EBA ML/TF Risk Factors Guidelines, Guideline 21.3(d)(i) and (ii), inserted by EBA/GL/2024/01

scenarios.title: Exposure to mixers, tumblers and decentralised platforms
scenarios.desc: Customers use or receive funds from platforms built to obfuscate transactions or that no legal or natural person controls.
scenarios.ref: EBA ML/TF Risk Factors Guidelines, Guideline 21.3(d)(iii) and (iv), inserted by EBA/GL/2024/01

scenarios.title: Transaction monitoring gaps: rule coverage, data quality, alert backlog
scenarios.desc: Scenarios do not cover the firm's real products and typologies, data feeds are incomplete, or alerts are not worked in time, so suspicious activity goes unseen.

scenarios.title: Incomplete payer and payee (or originator and beneficiary) information on transfers
scenarios.desc: Transfers of funds or crypto-assets arrive or leave without the required information and the firm does not detect or act on it.
scenarios.ref: Regulation (EU) 2023/1113 (transfers of funds and certain crypto-assets)

scenarios.title: Cash-based top-ups and cash-outs
scenarios.desc: Cash loaded or withdrawn through agents, ATMs or voucher networks hides the source or destination of funds.
scenarios.ref: For CASPs: EBA ML/TF Risk Factors Guidelines, Guideline 21.3(d)(v) (crypto-ATMs and similar hardware), inserted by EBA/GL/2024/01
